As we age, our skin undergoes myriad changes, becoming drier, thinner, and more prone to lines and wrinkles. While this means we demand more from our skincare, it also means you’ll be looking for a concealer better suited to more mature skin. While I like to think my own descent into ageing skin has only just started, the reality is that these days, I do need my concealer to work harder. Whether it’s worsening sleep habits causing deeper, darker circles in my increasingly fragile undereye area, more noticeable sunspots or an infuriating recurrence of hormonal spots, I need a concealer that really holds up. And stays put. Read more: Best eye creams for brightening and lifting, tested by a mature skin expert When it comes to texture, I personally prefer something on the creamier side so that it blends easily and doesn’t sit too heavily in fine lines and creases. It also needs to be fluid enough so that it doesn’t sit unnaturally atop blemishes and dry them out (they always look worse caked in product).

items.key: ai:how emilia clarke survived 2 brain haemorrhages: why recovery can take months
items.text: How Emilia Clarke survived 2 brain haemorrhages: Why recovery can take months
items.article: The actor’s experience highlights why being medically stable does not necessarily mean the brain has fully recovered. A neurologist explains what happens in the days, weeks and months after a haemorrhage When actor Emilia Clarke suffered a brain haemorrhage at the age of 24, surviving the immediate medical crisis was only the beginning of a much longer recovery. She underwent surgery and later spoke about experiencing problems with speech and memory. She suffered a second brain haemorrhage a few years later and has since spoken publicly about the long-term effects of brain injury and the importance of rehabilitation. Her experience highlights an important distinction in brain haemorrhage recovery: Being medically stable does not necessarily mean that a person has recovered from the injury. When a brain haemorrhage occurs, the immediate priority is to stop the bleeding, control pressure inside the skull and stabilise the patient. But once these concerns are addressed, another phase begins: recovery from the injury that the brain has already sustained. “A patient may, therefore, be medically stable but still have difficulty with movement, speech, memory, balance or other everyday functions. Recovery can continue for weeks or months, depending on the part of the brain affected and the extent of the injury,” Dr Vinit Suri, senior consultant, Neurology, Indraprastha Apollo Hospital, Delhi, told The Indian Express . items.text: How a 32-year-old writer turned her Substack into a $263,000 business: ‘It’s a side hustle’
items.article: Amy Suto started out as a television writer in Hollywood before moving into freelance writing and ghostwriting. A freelance writer has turned a newsletter, created to help fellow writers, into a business that now brings in more than $263,000 (around Rs 2.5 crore) in annual recurring revenue. Amy Suto, 32, a San Francisco resident, launched her Substack, “Make Writing Your Job”, in June 2023. What started as a place to answer questions about finding writing work has since expanded into a paid job board, online community, and resource platform. “Building our Substack has been an incredible bonus,” Suto told Business Insider. “It’s a side hustle, and my primary income still comes from freelance memoir ghostwriting.” According to Business Insider , the newsletter now has more than 58,000 subscribers. Business Insider reported Suto started out as a television writer in Hollywood before moving into freelance writing and ghostwriting. She later wrote a book about building a six-figure career as a freelance writer. The idea for her newsletter came from the questions she kept receiving about how she found clients and writing opportunities.

items.article: Bruno Fernandes has found his form again with Portugal and he could return to Man Utd ready to hit the ground running. In his first camp as Portugal head coach, the wily veteran Jorge Jesus has shown a willingness to take the tough decisions and ruffle a few feathers, and it could be that his approach benefits Manchester United . Whatever happens on the pitch, the headlines from Portugal's quartet of Nations League fixtures will all be about Cristiano Ronaldo and what looks like being a dramatic - and petulant - end to a distinguished international career. Any capital Ronaldo thought he might have pretty much evaporated on Thursday night, when Portugal swept aside Denmark 4-2 to maintain their 100% record in the Nations League. It's hard to see why they would return to the 41-year-old now. Jesus has taken the tough decisions that his predecessors couldn't, and he is the one who will likely reap the benefits. In the absence of Ronaldo, other star players are coming to the fore, and this feels like it's Bruno Fernandes' Portugal now, just as it should have been during the World Cup. In Copenhagen, Fernandes captained his country in a competitive game for the first time in a 96-cap career, and he delivered two breathtakingly good assists as well, setting up goals for Goncalo Ramos and Vitinha. items.article: Harriet said the decision had a major impact on her life - even though she does not regret it A woman has explained the massive impact stopping topical steroid creams to manage eczema after 20-plus years has had on her life. Harriet Williams, 33, was diagnosed with eczema as a child that continues to trigger itchiness across the "majority" of her body's skin. Her parents began administering topical steroids to Harriet at the age five after advice from specialist doctors, and she continued applying them for more than 20 years. Yet despite her efforts, Harriet kept getting "very aggressive" and "random" eczema flare-ups, which could be sparked by things like dust mites, weather changes, food and stress. Then, in 2020, Harriet said she realised her steroid use had given her skin a "paper look". So when the UK went into lockdown in the Covid-19 pandemic, she decided to reduce gradually her treatment that April. By early winter, Harriet said the symptoms of topical steroid withdrawal (TSW) struck "all at once" - including skin and hair loss, heightened itchiness, inability to control her body temperature and a "thick layer of skin" that developed across her entire body. She said it led to full-body skin hardness and burning sensations. Worse, she said she went "completely bald" and was confined to her house for seven months. items.article: Taking or considering weight-loss injections? GP reveals some sleep changes you might not expect From waking up with new hip pain to suddenly finding your mattress too firm, a GP has revealed five unexpected ways significant weight loss from injections like Wegovy and Mounjaro can affect your sleep. The number of adults using GLP-1 medications in Great Britain has nearly tripled in two years to 1.9 million , with 68% now taking them primarily for weight loss, according to research. But as the number of people using weight-loss medications continues to increase, health experts warn of some issues that may arise. Dr Roger Henderson , GP and medical expert for MattressNextDay , says one part of significant weight loss people may not expect to change is their sleep. And the consequences can go beyond simply feeling uncomfortable, he says. If you're struggling to settle, repeatedly changing position or waking from new aches or pressure points, those physical changes can begin to disrupt your sleep , too. Meanwhile, people taking GLP-1 medications may experience a separate set of sleep problems. The medical specialist warns that side effects like nausea, indigestion, acid reflux and abdominal discomfort can make it harder to get comfortable at night.
